STRENGTHS: (1) Real, well-articulated problem: cost-driven non-adherence among young adults with chronic conditions is credible, emotionally resonant and has clear downstream cost consequences. (2) Focused wedge: targeting 18-34 chronic-condition patients with plain-language onboarding and education is a sensible niche in an otherwise generic market. (3) Sensible product bundling: price comparison + multi-source discount identification + budgeting/refill reminders is a coherent value stack, and the free core product aligns with the target user's price sensitivity. (4) Execution evidence: a working prototype exists, first outside users are onboarded, entity is formed, and spend is lean (a few thousand dollars). (5) Self-awareness: founders candidly acknowledge unsigned referral deals, uncertain conversion, crowded competition and gaps in regulatory/privacy knowledge. (6) Reasonable ask and milestones: ~$75K to expand data, run a several-hundred-user pilot and measure savings and retention is a proportionate, testable next step. (7) Complementary team skills (public health, engineering, business/partnerships) with initial advisor feedback.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Weak differentiation and defensibility: GoodRx-style discount cards, pharmacy and insurer apps already dominate; the stated differentiators (niche focus, budgeting add-on, multi-source comparison) are easy for incumbents to replicate and no moat (data, network effects, proprietary partnerships) is identified. (2) Unproven monetization: referral revenue depends on unsigned agreements, and the target segment is low-income and low-spend per user, so referral yield per user is likely small; premium conversion assumptions are unquantified and the willingness to pay for budgeting is untested. (3) No validated traction: sample is small, no measured savings, retention, engagement or willingness to pay; the prototype uses limited, partly sample data, so the core promise (accurate real prices) is not yet demonstrated. (4) Data dependency risk: reliable, current pharmacy and discount pricing data is costly and hard to license, and accuracy errors would destroy trust. (5) Regulatory and privacy exposure: handling prescription and health data (HIPAA-adjacent, state privacy laws, pharmacy referral and anti-kickback considerations) is acknowledged but not addressed. (6) Market sizing and economics are vague: 'several million' users is unrefined, no CAC, LTV, unit economics or financial model, and distribution beyond campus channels is unclear (young adults churn quickly out of student status). (7) Team limitations: student founders without healthcare, pharmacy-benefits or regulated-data experience; no formal advisors; part-time commitment is unclear. (8) Secondary markets (campus health, employers, clinics) are untested and may require long sales cycles.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT: A thoughtful, honest, early-stage concept addressing a real problem with a modest, de-risking plan, but currently pre-validation with thin differentiation, an unproven revenue model and significant data/regulatory dependencies. Investment interest is moderate-to-low at this stage: attractive as a small, milestone-based bet, not yet compelling for institutional capital. Interest would rise materially with evidence of measured user savings, retention, at least one signed data or referral partner, and a clear compliance approach.

Business plan text:

Moneymeds
Moneymeds: Executive Summary
Problem
Many young adults with chronic conditions have to make difficult choices about their
medication. Aging off a parent's insurance plan, working part-time or gig jobs, or enrolling in
a high-deductible plan often leaves them paying a large share of prescription costs themselves.
Surveys of patients regularly report that a meaningful portion of people skip doses, split
pills or delay refills because of cost. For someone managing asthma, diabetes or a mental
health condition, these choices can lead to emergency visits that cost far more than the
medication would have.
The tools that could help are fragmented. The cash price of one prescription can differ a great
deal from one pharmacy to the next, even within a single neighborhood. Discount cards,
manufacturer savings coupons, patient assistance programs and pharmacy loyalty programs each
have their own rules, and no single place tells a patient which one to use. Young adults in
particular are often new to managing their own health costs and have had little guidance on how
to do it.
Solution
Moneymeds is a mobile app that does three things in one place. First, it compares prescription
prices across nearby pharmacies based on the user's medications and location. Second, it
identifies which discount program or coupon applies and shows the resulting price, so the user
does not have to test several cards at the counter. Third, it offers a simple monthly health
budget that accounts for refills, copays, deductibles and upcoming appointments, and sends
reminders before a refill is due so users can shop around ahead of time.
The app is designed for people who are not experts in healthcare. We use plain language, short
onboarding and a focus on the few decisions that matter most: where to fill a prescription,
which program to use and how much to set aside each month. We also include short educational
content explaining terms such as deductible, formulary and generic substitution, since many of
our target users have never had to learn them.
Market
Our target customers are U.S. adults ages 18 to 34 with at least one chronic condition
requiring ongoing prescription medication. Public health data suggests that a substantial share
of young adults live with a chronic condition, and a large portion of them report some
difficulty affording care. We estimate that several million people fall in this group
nationally, though we have not yet refined this figure. Our initial focus is students and
recent graduates in the region around our university, where we can reach users through campus
health centers, student groups and local clinics.
Beyond individual consumers, we see secondary markets in campus health services, employers who
want to support younger employees, and community clinics that help patients find affordable
medication. We have not yet tested interest in any of these.
Business Model
We plan to earn revenue in two ways. The first is referral fees paid by discount program
providers and pharmacies when a user fills a prescription through a Moneymeds recommendation.
The second is a premium subscription of a few dollars per month offering features such as
family sharing, expanded budgeting tools and refill planning across multiple medications. The
core price comparison would remain free so that cost is never a barrier for the users we most
want to reach.
We recognize that referral revenue depends on agreements we have not yet signed, and that

conversion from free to paid is uncertain. Our current financial thinking assumes modest early
revenue from referrals and a small share of users converting to the premium tier, and we intend
to refine these assumptions with pilot data. Our main costs will be software development, data
licensing for pharmacy prices and basic cloud infrastructure.
Competition
The prescription savings space is crowded. Several well-known discount card and coupon services
already let people look up prices and print or show a card at the pharmacy. Large pharmacy
chains and insurers have their own apps, and some online pharmacies offer low-cost generics by
mail. Most of these services are designed for the general population and earn money by taking a
share of each transaction.
We believe Moneymeds can differentiate itself in three ways. First, we focus on young adults
with chronic conditions rather than all consumers, which lets us tailor the experience and the
education to their situation. Second, we combine price comparison with budgeting, whereas most
competitors stop at the pharmacy counter. Third, we compare across several discount sources
rather than promoting a single one. We acknowledge that larger competitors could add similar
features, and that our advantage will depend on how well we understand and serve this specific
group.
Team
Priya Raman, chief executive officer, is a senior studying public health. She has volunteered
at a campus health center and leads product direction and user research. Daniel Okafor, chief
technology officer, is a computer science senior who built the first version of the app and
manages development and data integration. Maya Lindqvist, chief operating officer, is a junior
in business administration who handles partnerships, outreach and early financial planning. We
have also had informal conversations with a faculty member in health policy and a local
pharmacist, who have offered feedback but are not formally involved.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined our core concept and formed a Delaware C corporation. We have built a working
prototype that compares prices for a limited set of common medications using publicly available
and sample data. We launched the prototype with our first outside users, a small group of
students recruited through campus contacts, and have begun collecting feedback on how they use
it. Early comments suggest users value seeing price differences and want better budgeting
reminders, though our sample is small and we have not yet measured savings or retention. We
have a basic website describing the product.
To date we have spent only a few thousand dollars, funded by the founders, mainly on legal
formation, hosting and data access. We have no revenue. Over the next twelve months we expect
to need roughly seventy-five thousand dollars to expand data coverage, improve the app, run a
larger pilot and begin discussions with discount providers about referral agreements. We have
not yet built a detailed financial model beyond these estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for funding, mentorship and connections. Prize money would
go toward licensing more complete pharmacy price data and running a pilot with several hundred
users. We would especially value guidance from mentors with experience in healthcare
regulation, privacy and partnership agreements, since we are still learning how to handle
sensitive health information responsibly. We would also welcome introductions to campus health
centers, clinics and potential discount program partners. Our goal for the coming year is to
show that users save real money and keep using the app, which would give us a stronger basis
for raising outside investment.
